source_metadata.title: Information Abundance Paradox: Long-Context Training Undermines Parametric Knowledge

atoms.canonical_statement: The study tests whether increasing train-time context shifts language models from parametric internalization toward contextualization rather than acting only as a neutral data-delivery mechanism.

The authors test the Information Abundance Paradox across natural-language pretraining, supervised fine-tuning, a theoretical information-frontier analysis, synthetic pretraining, gradient allocation, module-restricted interventions, and inference-time attention.

The Information Abundance Paradox is the hypothesis that task-relevant information available in the training context can reduce the incentive to encode that information in model parameters, shifting learning toward contextualization.
The paper defines context addiction as strong performance when useful context is available together with deterioration when context is absent or misleading.

The motivating comparison evaluates Phi-3 3.8B and 14B short-context 4K versus long-context 128K instruction-tuned variants, and OLMo 3 7B and 32B short-context 8K versus long-context 65K base-model variants.
Across the reported Phi-3 and OLMo 3 comparisons, long-context variants were significantly worse in 20 of 23 benchmark-setting comparisons.

population.label: 23 reported long-context versus short-context benchmark-setting comparisons

concept.text: Statistically significant underperformance of the long-context variant

quantitative_result.original_result_text: long-context variants are significantly worse in 20 of the 23 reported comparisons

atoms.canonical_statement: Natural-language pretraining uses Llama-2-style decoder-only models at 20M, 55M, 259M, and 750M parameters.
Natural-language pretraining uses 10 billion training tokens from a Project Gutenberg subset restricted to documents containing at least 65,536 tokens.

Within each model scale, the pretraining context window is swept over seven powers of two from 512 to 32,768 tokens while keeping the corpus, model initialization, optimizer, token budget, and optimization-step count matched.

Every natural-language pretraining variant processes about 1.05 million tokens per optimization step for 9,537 optimization steps, yielding a token-and-update-matched comparison rather than a FLOP-matched comparison.
Natural-language pretraining evaluation is zero-shot and covers a language-modeling suite, SuperGLUE, and a closed-book multiple-choice QA suite without auxiliary context.
The closed-book MCQA suite includes ARC-Easy, ARC-Challenge, CommonsenseQA, HellaSwag, OpenBookQA, PIQA, SocialIQA, MedQA, TruthfulQA, SciQ, and WinoGrande.
Natural-language pretraining uses multiple random seeds: five seeds for the 20M model and three seeds for the 55M, 259M, and 750M models, with evaluation results averaged across seeds.

Across model scales, SuperGLUE and closed-book MCQA accuracy follow an inverted-U trajectory with train-time context length, while language-modeling cross-entropy follows a corresponding U-shaped trajectory.

Aggregate SuperGLUE and closed-book MCQA performance peak around a 2,048-token pretraining window, whereas aggregate language-modeling performance peaks around 8,192 tokens before degrading at longer windows.
Segmented-regression inflection tests are significant for language modeling, SuperGLUE, and MCQA at every tested model scale from 20M through 750M parameters.
The same qualitative context-length trend appears with RoPE, ALiBi, and LongRoPE positional encoding in the 259M-model ablation.
Per-dataset language-modeling results on LAMBADA, PTB, and WikiSPAN show improvement at shorter-to-intermediate training windows followed by degradation at longer windows.
Per-dataset closed-book MCQA results show the same broad improve-then-degrade pattern as the aggregate MCQA curve, indicating that the effect is not solely an averaging artifact.
PTB, LAMBADA, and WikiSPAN have mean example lengths of 28, 88, and 504 tokens and attain their best reported language-modeling loss at training windows of 512, 2,048, and 8,192 tokens, respectively.
MCQA and SuperGLUE have mean example lengths of 65 and 135 tokens, respectively, and both show reported inflection at a 2,048-token training window.
For the 259M pretraining model, average training cost rises from 27.90 GPU-hours at a 512-token context window to 83.44 GPU-hours at a 32K-token context window.

population.label: 259M-parameter natural-language pretraining model

atoms.canonical_statement: Supervised fine-tuning uses Qwen3 models at 0.6B, 1.7B, 4B, 8B, and 14B parameters on MMLU-Pro Health, Economics, Law, and Psychology.
Because MMLU-Pro provides only a test split, each selected domain is partitioned into 80% fine-tuning examples and 20% held-out evaluation examples.
SFT holds the prepended context budget fixed at eight documents and varies the number of target-domain documents k over 0, 4, and 8, with the remaining documents drawn from a paired other domain.

Supporting and conflicting documents are generated with gemini-3.1-flash-lite-preview; supporting documents favor the correct answer while conflicting documents are designed to plausibly steer toward a likely incorrect answer.
SFT evaluation uses three conditions: supporting target-domain context, conflicting target-domain context, and no prepended context, with deterministic generation and exact-match accuracy.
SFT trains for five epochs with learning rate 1e-4, cosine decay, gradient clipping at 1.0, maximum sequence length 1,024, and LoRA rank 64 with alpha 128.
Supporting and conflicting SFT contexts occupy similar few-hundred-token length ranges, so the intended manipulation is context relevance/composition rather than gross context length.
For Qwen3-0.6B, increasing target-domain training context from k=0 to k=8 changes no-context accuracy by -5.4 percentage points.

atoms.canonical_statement: Across the full SFT results, increasing target-domain context during fine-tuning generally improves supporting-context accuracy while reducing robustness when context is absent or conflicting across domains and model sizes.
The theoretical analysis defines the parametric information frontier I_k(rho) as the infimum of mutual information I(W;tau) needed to attain risk at most rho when the predictor has context size k.
Under nested inputs, the paper proves that the parametric information frontier is monotone non-increasing with context size: for k<m, I_m(rho) <= I_k(rho).

The theoretical result is an achievability statement: longer context can reduce the minimum task information that must be stored in weights to meet a fixed risk threshold, but it does not by itself prove that a specific optimizer will choose that solution.
The synthetic pretraining study uses unary bitwise operations, string transformations, digit-wise mod10 arithmetic, and Caesar cipher tasks at 0.3M, 1.5M, and 7.5M parameter model scales.
Synthetic datasets contain about 33,000 training examples and 10,000 disjoint test examples per task, and the training-set size is held fixed across numbers of in-context demonstrations.

Synthetic evaluation compares supporting versus consistent-but-incorrect conflicting demonstrations, using the supporting-minus-conflicting performance gap as the context-addiction measure; no-context evaluation is omitted because removing demonstrations would be out-of-distribution.

In the 7.5M synthetic models, context addiction grows with more train-time demonstrations for bitwise and string tasks, remains stable for mod10, and shows only a localized longest-context deviation for Caesar cipher.
For Bitwise operations, the Kendall trend between increasing demonstrations and mean training gradient norm is tau=-0.409.

atoms.canonical_statement: Across synthetic model scales, tasks showing larger supporting-conflicting gaps also show lower average training gradient norms with more demonstrations, and context addiction becomes stronger as model size grows.

The module-level analysis averages gradient norms within feed-forward-network and self-attention module types, computes the FFN-to-SA gradient-norm ratio at each step, and averages that ratio over training steps.
In SFT, k=8 task-relevant context produces a lower FFN-to-SA gradient-norm ratio than no-context tuning in all 20 model-domain comparisons, with 19 of 20 differences statistically significant.
For the 20M pretraining model, the mean FFN-to-SA gradient-norm-ratio slope is -0.038 per doubling of context length.

atoms.canonical_statement: Module-restricted intervention results show that FFN-only tuning is more robust to absent or conflicting context, whereas SA-only tuning improves supporting-context performance and increases sensitivity to conflicting context.

Inference-time context attention is measured as normalized attention mass from generated answer-token queries to prepended document tokens, averaged over answer positions and examples and summarized by the maximum-attending head within each layer.

atoms.canonical_statement: Qwen3-0.6B, 1.7B, 8B, and 14B models fine-tuned with task-relevant context show greater inference-time attention to supplied context than corresponding no-context-trained models, with the largest differences in middle layers.

The authors state that the natural-language pretraining experiments are limited to models up to 750M parameters and that larger-scale testing is needed to determine how inflection location and severity change with model size, data scale, and compute.

The authors conclude that train-time context is not a neutral scaling axis: increasing context can shift learning from parametric internalization toward contextualization, so long-context capability should be considered together with context-independent competence.
